$V_v=\mathbb C^v$. A **framed datum** is a pair of complex-linear maps

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (w) at (0,0) {$W=\mathbb C$};
  \node (v) at (3,0) {$V_v$};
  \draw[->] (w) to[bend left=22] node[above] {$I$} (v);
  \draw[->] (v) to[bend left=22] node[below] {$J$} (w);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

[[def-affine-scheme-spectrum]]. An orbit of stable data maps to the point
whose prime ideal consists of invariant functions vanishing on that orbit;

$\mathcal L(v,1)=\pi_v^{-1}(0)$.

zero framing maps. A framed subdatum with vertex space $V'=0$ uses the same
framing space $W$ and zero maps $I':W\to0$ and $J':0\to W$. Its inclusion

space $0$ and vertex space $V_1$, so its induced framing maps vanish and it is

$\mathfrak M(0,1)\times\mathfrak M(1,1)$ obtained this way. Its two projection
maps are the source and target maps of the correspondence.

using [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]] and
[[thm-singular-homology-satisfies-dimension-and-arbitrary-additivity]]. When
$P_{0,1}$ and both spaces are points and the projections are identities,
define its fundamental-class correspondence map to send the source point
class to the target point class; the reverse map uses the same rule. This is
the point push-pull convention used here.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $H$ be a unital associative
$R$-algebra. An **$R$-linear representation of $H$** on an $R$-module $M$ is
a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism
$\rho:H\to\operatorname{End}_R(M)$, where $\operatorname{End}_R(M)$ is the
ring of $R$-linear maps $M\to M$, with composition as multiplication,
$\operatorname{id}_M$ as unit, and scalar map $r\mapsto r\operatorname{id}_M$.
It defines the unital left action
$h\cdot m:=\rho(h)(m)$; its module axioms are those of
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]. When $H$ is a Hall algebra, this structure is
called a **Hall-algebra module**.

This term does not mean an object of the input category. An input object $A$
contributes a basis symbol $[A]$ to a Hall algebra, but that symbol by itself
specifies no representation on an $R$-module. The untwisted Hall algebra
instance is supplied by
[[def-untwisted-hall-algebra]],
[[thm-untwisted-hall-algebra-is-associative-and-unital]].

The zero $R$-module is allowed; its identity endomorphism is its zero map.
This definition gives an algebra action only. An action on a tensor product
requires additional structure, such as a specified coproduct.

derivations.claim: Define $\rho(a)(h)=ah$ for $a,h\in H$. Since multiplication is $R$-bilinear, for each fixed $a$ the map $h\mapsto ah$ is $R$-linear and $a\mapsto\rho(a)$ is $R$-linear, so $\rho:H\to\operatorname{End}_R(H)$ is an $R$-linear map.

For $a,b,h\in H$, $\rho(ab)(h)=(ab)h=a(bh)=(\rho(a)\circ\rho(b))(h)$ by associativity, and $\rho(1_H)(h)=1_Hh=h$, so $\rho(1_H)=\operatorname{id}_H$. Thus $\rho$ is a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism and hence a Hall-algebra representation by [F1].

Let $k=\mathbb F_q$, and let $I_\lambda$ denote the nilpotent Jordan-quiver
representation indexed by a partition $\lambda$, as in
[[lem-jordan-quiver-isoclasses-are-partition-indexed]]. For partitions
$\mu,\nu,\lambda$, let $g^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q)$ be the coefficient of
$[I_\lambda]$ in the untwisted product $[I_\mu]*[I_\nu]$. There are
polynomials $G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(t)\in\mathbb Z[t]$, independent of the
finite field, with
$$ g^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q)=G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q). $$
A coefficient is zero unless $|\lambda|=|\mu|+|\nu|$.

Define the **generic Jordan-quiver Hall algebra** by
$$ H_{\mathrm{gen}}:=\bigoplus_\lambda\mathbb Z[t]u_\lambda, \qquad u_\mu*u_\nu:=\sum_\lambda G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(t)u_\lambda, $$
giving $u_\lambda$ degree $|\lambda|$ and $t$ degree $0$.
The size condition above makes this a graded algebra.
Then $H_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is a commutative associative unital algebra and a free
polynomial algebra over $\mathbb Z[t]$ on the classes
$u_{(1^r)}$, $r\ge1$. After extending scalars to
$\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, the assignment
$$ \Phi_t(u_{(1^r)})=t^{-r(r-1)/2}e_r $$
for every $r\ge1$, and $\Phi_t(u_\varnothing)=1$, extends uniquely to a
graded algebra isomorphism
$$ H_{\mathrm{gen}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z[t]}\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}] \;\cong\; \Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}], $$
where $\Lambda$ is the stable graded ring of symmetric functions.

Extend the generic Jordan Hall algebra of
[[thm-generic-jordan-hall-algebra-is-symmetric-functions]] to $\mathbb Q(t)$,
and use **that theorem's exact map**
$\Phi_t(u_{(1^r)})=t^{-\binom r2}e_r$.
Let $n(\lambda)$ and $b_\lambda(s)$ have the conventions of
[[def-hall-littlewood-scalar-product-and-functions]], and put
$$ a_\lambda(t)=t^{|\lambda|+2n(\lambda)}b_\lambda(t^{-1}). $$
Define the Jordan **Green pairing** to be the bilinear form
$$ (u_\lambda,u_\mu)_G=\delta_{\lambda\mu}a_\lambda(t)^{-1}. $$
It is nondegenerate and equals inverse automorphism counting at every
finite-field specialization $t=q$.
Then the Hall–Littlewood functions exist uniquely in the monic
orthogonal convention specified there, and
$$ \Phi_t(u_\lambda)=t^{-n(\lambda)}P_\lambda(x;t^{-1}),\qquad \langle P_\lambda,P_\mu\rangle_s=\delta_{\lambda\mu}b_\lambda(s)^{-1}. $$
More precisely, if $f,g\in\Lambda^d_{\mathbb Q(t)}$, then
$$ (\Phi_t^{-1}f,\Phi_t^{-1}g)_G=t^{-d}\langle f,g\rangle_{t^{-1}}. $$
Different degrees are orthogonal. In particular the transported pairing on
power sums is
$$ (\Phi_t^{-1}p_\lambda,\Phi_t^{-1}p_\mu)_G=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda\prod_i(t^{\lambda_i}-1)^{-1}. $$
The empty partition gives $1$, with norm $1$. All the displayed basis and
pairing identities specialize at $t=q>1$ and at $s=q^{-1}$.
The pairing normalization is a degree scaling of the standard
Hall–Littlewood form; it is not the ordinary symmetric-function Hall inner
product.

For $r\ge1$, let $p_r\in\Lambda^r$ be the compatible sequence of finite
power-sum polynomials $p_r(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=\sum_{i=1}^N x_i^r$
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]],
[[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]). For a
partition $\lambda$, set $p_\lambda:=\prod_i p_{\lambda_i}$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Write
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$ and
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda^d$. Then
$$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\ldots],$$
and for every $d\ge0$, the family $\{p_\lambda:\lambda\vdash d\}$ is a
$\mathbb Q$-basis of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$. These families are not in
general $\mathbb Z$-bases of $\Lambda^d$: in degree two,
$h_2=\tfrac12(p_{(1,1)}+p_{(2)})$ has nonintegral coordinates in the power-sum
basis.

Let $k$ be a field and $n\geq 1$. The **Heisenberg Lie algebra** $\mathfrak h_n(k)$ is the $(2n+1)$-dimensional $k$-vector space with basis

$$X_1,\ldots,X_n,P_1,\ldots,P_n,Z.$$

Its bracket is the bilinear extension of

$$[P_i,X_j]=\delta_{ij}Z,\qquad [X_i,P_j]=-\delta_{ij}Z,$$

with all $[X_i,X_j]$, $[P_i,P_j]$, $[Z,X_i]$, and $[Z,P_i]$ equal to zero. Here $\delta_{ij}=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Equivalently, for coefficient vectors $a,b,a',b'\in k^n$,

$$\left[\sum_i(a_iX_i+b_iP_i)+cZ,\sum_i(a_i'X_i+b_i'P_i)+c'Z\right]=\left(\sum_i(b_i a_i'-b_i'a_i)\right)Z.$$

The Jacobi identity and alternation, including in characteristic $2$, are proved in [[lem-heisenberg-bracket-defines-lie-algebra]].
For every field $k$ and integer $n\geq 1$, the vector space and bracket specified in [[def-heisenberg-lie-algebra]] form a Lie algebra over $k$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit, and let $H$ be any unital associative
$R$-algebra that is a Hall algebra. The map
$\rho:H\to\operatorname{End}_R(H)$ given by $\rho(a)(h)=ah$ is a
representation, so the left regular action makes $H$ a Hall-algebra module.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F5], scalar extension of the generic Hall algebra acts on its regular module by multiplication; extending the isomorphism [F1] from $\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$ to $K$ identifies this action with multiplication by $p_n$ when the Hall element $\Phi_t^{-1}(p_n)$ acts. Thus $X_n$ is the transported regular action. By [F2]–[F3], the power sums form an orthogonal basis with nonzero norms, since $z_\lambda\ne0$ and $t^r-1\ne0$ in $K$ for every part $r\ge1$. For partitions $\alpha,\beta$, both adjoint pairings vanish unless $\beta$ is obtained by adjoining one part $n$ to $\alpha$; in that case, if $m=m_n(\alpha)$, then $z_\beta=n(m+1)z_\alpha$ and $(X_np_\alpha,p_\beta)_G=(p_\alpha,X_n^{\dagger,G}p_\beta)_G=n(m+1)(t^n-1)^{-1}(p_\alpha,p_\alpha)_G$. Thus the displayed operator is the adjoint on every pair of basis elements, hence on all of $\Lambda_K$.

The formula in the Statement gives $P_np_\lambda=m_n(\lambda)p_{\lambda\setminus(n)}$, the formal derivative $\partial p_\lambda/\partial p_n$ by [F3], with value zero when $m_n(\lambda)=0$. Therefore the $P_n$ commute, the $X_n$ commute, and $P_n1=0$.

For any $m,n\ge1$ and basis monomial $p_\lambda$, the polynomial product rule gives $(P_nX_m-X_mP_n)p_\lambda=\delta_{nm}p_\lambda$. Since the $p_\lambda$ form a basis by [F3], $[P_n,X_m]=\delta_{nm}\operatorname{id}$. Together with the commuting relations of step 1.2 these are precisely the generator brackets in [F4].

For $1\le i\le N$, send $X_i,P_i,Z$ in $\mathfrak h_N(K)$ to multiplication by $p_i$, $\partial/\partial p_i$, and $\operatorname{id}$, respectively. Step 2.1 and the commuting relations in step 1.2 preserve every defining bracket, so the assignments give a Lie algebra representation. For any nonnegative integers $m_1,\ldots,m_N$, the monomial $p_1^{m_1}\cdots p_N^{m_N}$ is $\prod_{i=1}^N X_i^{m_i}1$; hence these vectors span $K[p_1,\ldots,p_N]$ and, as $N$ varies, generate $\Lambda_K$.

Let $k=\mathbb F_q$, and let $I_\lambda$ denote the nilpotent Jordan-quiver
representation indexed by a partition $\lambda$, as in
[[lem-jordan-quiver-isoclasses-are-partition-indexed]]. For partitions
$\mu,\nu,\lambda$, let $g^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q)$ be the coefficient of
$[I_\lambda]$ in the untwisted product $[I_\mu]*[I_\nu]$. There are
polynomials $G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(t)\in\mathbb Z[t]$, independent of the
finite field, with
$$ g^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q)=G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(q). $$
A coefficient is zero unless $|\lambda|=|\mu|+|\nu|$.

Define the **generic Jordan-quiver Hall algebra** by
$$ H_{\mathrm{gen}}:=\bigoplus_\lambda\mathbb Z[t]u_\lambda, \qquad u_\mu*u_\nu:=\sum_\lambda G^\lambda_{\mu,\nu}(t)u_\lambda, $$
giving $u_\lambda$ degree $|\lambda|$ and $t$ degree $0$.
The size condition above makes this a graded algebra.
Then $H_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is a commutative associative unital algebra and a free
polynomial algebra over $\mathbb Z[t]$ on the classes
$u_{(1^r)}$, $r\ge1$. After extending scalars to
$\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$, the assignment
$$ \Phi_t(u_{(1^r)})=t^{-r(r-1)/2}e_r $$
for every $r\ge1$, and $\Phi_t(u_\varnothing)=1$, extends uniquely to a
graded algebra isomorphism
$$ H_{\mathrm{gen}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z[t]}\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}] \;\cong\; \Lambda\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}], $$
where $\Lambda$ is the stable graded ring of symmetric functions.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $H$ be a unital associative
$R$-algebra. An **$R$-linear representation of $H$** on an $R$-module $M$ is
a unital $R$-algebra homomorphism
$\rho:H\to\operatorname{End}_R(M)$, where $\operatorname{End}_R(M)$ is the
ring of $R$-linear maps $M\to M$, with composition as multiplication,
$\operatorname{id}_M$ as unit, and scalar map $r\mapsto r\operatorname{id}_M$.
It defines the unital left action
$h\cdot m:=\rho(h)(m)$; its module axioms are those of
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]. When $H$ is a Hall algebra, this structure is
called a **Hall-algebra module**.

This term does not mean an object of the input category. An input object $A$
contributes a basis symbol $[A]$ to a Hall algebra, but that symbol by itself
specifies no representation on an $R$-module. The untwisted Hall algebra
instance is supplied by
[[def-untwisted-hall-algebra]],
[[thm-untwisted-hall-algebra-is-associative-and-unital]].

The zero $R$-module is allowed; its identity endomorphism is its zero map.
This definition gives an algebra action only. An action on a tensor product
requires additional structure, such as a specified coproduct.

The actions differ because $\rho_0(u_1)=0$ while $\rho_1(u_1)=\operatorname{id}_K$. Thus the same one-dimensional vector space carries two different Hall-module structures.

The **Hall inner product** is the graded $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form on the
stable ring $\Lambda$ ([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]])
characterized by
$$\langle h_\lambda,m_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}$$
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[thm-elementary-and-complete-families-freely-generate-the-stable-ring]],
[[thm-monomial-symmetric-functions-form-the-integral-stable-basis]]), where
$\delta_{\lambda\mu}=1$ if $\lambda=\mu$ and $0$ otherwise. In particular,
homogeneous components of unequal degrees are orthogonal.
For the empty partition, $h_\varnothing=m_\varnothing=1$, so
$\langle1,1\rangle_H=1$.

For each $d\ge0$, the proven integral bases give unique finite expansions
$$f_d=\sum_{\lambda\vdash d}a_\lambda h_\lambda,\qquad g_d=\sum_{\mu\vdash d}b_\mu m_\mu$$
for $f_d,g_d\in\Lambda^d$. Define their degree-$d$ pairing by
$$\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H:=\sum_{\lambda,\mu\vdash d}a_\lambda b_\mu\delta_{\lambda\mu}.$$
For $f=\sum_d f_d$ and $g=\sum_d g_d$ in the algebraic direct sum $\Lambda$,
set $$\langle f,g\rangle_H:=\sum_d\langle f_d,g_d\rangle_H.$$
Only finitely many $d$ contribute because $f$ and $g$ have finite degree
support. The unique expansions in the two integral bases make this a
well-defined $\mathbb Z$-bilinear form; the displayed basis rule determines it
uniquely on all of $\Lambda$.

Extend the Hall form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$ on $\Lambda$
$\mathbb Q$-bilinearly to
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$. For partitions
$\lambda$ and $\mu$, let
$$z_\lambda:=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!,\qquad m_r(\lambda):=\#\{i:\lambda_i=r\}.$$
Then
$$\langle p_\lambda,p_\mu\rangle_H=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda.$$
In particular, power sums of unequal degrees are orthogonal.

Extend the generic Jordan Hall algebra of
[[thm-generic-jordan-hall-algebra-is-symmetric-functions]] to $\mathbb Q(t)$,
and use **that theorem's exact map**
$\Phi_t(u_{(1^r)})=t^{-\binom r2}e_r$.
Let $n(\lambda)$ and $b_\lambda(s)$ have the conventions of
[[def-hall-littlewood-scalar-product-and-functions]], and put
$$ a_\lambda(t)=t^{|\lambda|+2n(\lambda)}b_\lambda(t^{-1}). $$
Define the Jordan **Green pairing** to be the bilinear form
$$ (u_\lambda,u_\mu)_G=\delta_{\lambda\mu}a_\lambda(t)^{-1}. $$
It is nondegenerate and equals inverse automorphism counting at every
finite-field specialization $t=q$.
Then the Hall–Littlewood functions exist uniquely in the monic
orthogonal convention specified there, and
$$ \Phi_t(u_\lambda)=t^{-n(\lambda)}P_\lambda(x;t^{-1}),\qquad \langle P_\lambda,P_\mu\rangle_s=\delta_{\lambda\mu}b_\lambda(s)^{-1}. $$
More precisely, if $f,g\in\Lambda^d_{\mathbb Q(t)}$, then
$$ (\Phi_t^{-1}f,\Phi_t^{-1}g)_G=t^{-d}\langle f,g\rangle_{t^{-1}}. $$
Different degrees are orthogonal. In particular the transported pairing on
power sums is
$$ (\Phi_t^{-1}p_\lambda,\Phi_t^{-1}p_\mu)_G=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda\prod_i(t^{\lambda_i}-1)^{-1}. $$
The empty partition gives $1$, with norm $1$. All the displayed basis and
pairing identities specialize at $t=q>1$ and at $s=q^{-1}$.
The pairing normalization is a degree scaling of the standard
Hall–Littlewood form; it is not the ordinary symmetric-function Hall inner
product.

Use the category of finite-dimensional nilpotent Jordan-quiver representations from [[def-jordan-quiver-nilpotent-representation-category]]. Let $t$ be an indeterminate, $K=\mathbb Q(t)$, and $H_{J,K}:=H_{\mathrm{gen}}\otimes_{\mathbb Z[t]}K$ be the generic Jordan-quiver Hall algebra extended to $K$. Extend the exact isomorphism
$\Phi_t$ of [[thm-generic-jordan-hall-algebra-is-symmetric-functions]] to
$K$; its regular module is identified with
$\Lambda_K:=K\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda=K[p_1,p_2,\ldots]$. For a partition
$\lambda$, let $m_r(\lambda)$ be the multiplicity of $r$, set
$p_\lambda=\prod_{r\ge1}p_r^{m_r(\lambda)}$ and
$z_\lambda=\prod_{r\ge1}r^{m_r(\lambda)}m_r(\lambda)!$, and put
$p_\varnothing=1$. Write $\lambda\setminus(n)$ for the partition obtained
by removing one part $n$ when $m_n(\lambda)>0$; define
$m_n(\lambda)p_{\lambda\setminus(n)}=0$ when $m_n(\lambda)=0$. Transport
the Jordan Green pairing of
[[thm-jordan-hall-pairing-and-hall-littlewood-basis]] to $\Lambda_K$. On
power sums it is
$$(p_\lambda,p_\mu)_G=\delta_{\lambda\mu}z_\lambda\prod_i(t^{\lambda_i}-1)^{-1},$$
where $\delta_{\lambda\mu}=1$ if $\lambda=\mu$ and $0$ otherwise, and the
product runs over the parts of $\lambda$ with multiplicity. For $n\ge1$, let
$X_n$ be multiplication by $p_n$ and define
$$X_n^{\dagger,G}p_\lambda=\frac{n\,m_n(\lambda)}{t^n-1}p_{\lambda\setminus(n)},\qquad P_n:=\frac{t^n-1}{n}X_n^{\dagger,G}.$$
Then $X_n^{\dagger,G}$ is the adjoint of $X_n$ for $(\ ,\ )_G$,
$P_n=\partial/\partial p_n$, and for each finite $N\ge1$ the assignments
$X_i\mapsto (p_i\text{-multiplication})$, $P_i\mapsto\partial/\partial p_i$,
and $Z\mapsto\operatorname{id}$ give a representation of the finite
Heisenberg Lie algebra $\mathfrak h_N(K)$ from
[[def-heisenberg-lie-algebra]]. The constant $1$ is the vacuum: $P_n1=0$,
and the vectors $\prod_{i=1}^N X_i^{m_i}1$, with nonnegative integer
exponents, span the subalgebra $K[p_1,\ldots,p_N]$; as $N$ varies, they span
$\Lambda_K$.

derivations.claim: The Hall norm formula in [F1] gives $\langle p_1^r,p_1^r\rangle_H=r!$ because $z_{(1^r)}=r!$; the Green norm in [F2] gives $(p_1^r,p_1^r)_G=r!(t-1)^{-r}$. At $r=0$ both are $1$ by the empty-product convention.

For either form and any power-sum monomial $p_\mu$ of degree $r-1$, orthogonality makes the pairing of $p_1p_\mu$ with $p_1^r$ vanish unless $\mu=(1^{r-1})$. Nondegenerate diagonal norms then force each adjoint image of $p_1^r$ to be a multiple of $p_1^{r-1}$. Comparing against that monomial gives $X_1^{\dagger,H}p_1^r=rp_1^{r-1}$ and $X_1^{\dagger,G}p_1^r=\frac{r}{t-1}p_1^{r-1}$.
By [F3], $P_1=(t-1)X_1^{\dagger,G}$, so $P_1p_1^r=rp_1^{r-1}$, the same as the standard Hall adjoint. At $r=0$ the degree-lowering adjoints send $1$ to zero.

citations.quote: Let $V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over $k$. For $0\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ denotes the parameter set of $r$-dimensional linear subspaces of $V$. Thus $\operatorname{Gr}(0,V)=\{0\}$ and $\operatorname{Gr}(n,V)=\{V\}$. For $r<0$ or $r>n$ we set $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)=\varnothing$.

For every $r$-subset $I$ of a basis of an $n$-dimensional $V$, the locus $p_I\ne0$ in $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf A_k^{r(n-r)}$; these loci cover the Grassmannian and have regular transition maps.
For $0\le r\le n$, $\operatorname{Gr}(r,V)$ is smooth in the elementary local-affine-chart sense, irreducible, and has dimension $r(n-r)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the relative Proj and sheaf
constructions ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $S$ be a scheme, let $E$ be a
finite locally free $\mathcal O_S$-module of locally constant rank
([[def-locally-free-sheaf-finite-rank]]), and let
$$\pi:\mathbb P_S(E)=\operatorname{Proj}_S\operatorname{Sym}(E)\longrightarrow S$$
be its projective bundle in the quotient convention, with twist
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_S(E)}(1)$ and tautological quotient
$\pi^*E\to\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_S(E)}(1)$
([[def-projective-bundle-scheme]],
[[def-relative-proj-quasi-coherent-graded-algebra]]).

Then for every $S$-scheme $g:T\to S$ the assignment
$$h\longmapsto\Bigl(h^*\bigl(\pi^*E\to\mathcal O_{\mathbb P_S(E)}(1)\bigr)\Bigr)$$
is a natural bijection between

1. the set of $S$-morphisms $h:T\to\mathbb P_S(E)$, and
2. the set of isomorphism classes of surjections $g^*E\to L$ with $L$ an
   invertible $\mathcal O_T$-module ([[def-invertible-sheaf]]), where an
   isomorphism between $g^*E\to L$ and $g^*E\to L'$ is an isomorphism
   $L\to L'$ of $\mathcal O_T$-modules making the triangle commute.

Naturality means compatibility with morphisms $T'\to T$ of $S$-schemes. For
$T=\mathbb P_S(E)$ and $h=\operatorname{id}$ the class on the right is the
tautological quotient itself: $\operatorname{id}^*(\pi^*E\to\mathcal O(1))$ is
$\pi^*E\to\mathcal O(1)$. The rank-zero case is included: if $E=0$ then
$\mathbb P_S(0)=\varnothing$, and the two sides are empty for nonempty $T$ and
singletons for $T=\varnothing$.

derivations.claim: Stability and $IJ=0$ give $S=\operatorname{im}J$ of dimension $v$ and $A=JI$ with image in $S$ and $A|_S=0$. Conversely such $(S,A)$ and a frame $j:V\xrightarrow{\sim}S$ give $J=j$ followed by inclusion and $I=j^{-1}A$. These constructions are inverse and algebraic on the graph charts [F1]; changing the frame is exactly the free $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ action. The stable locus is therefore the frame bundle over the displayed vector bundle, proving the algebraic geometric quotient claim, without an appeal to an unspecified GIT quotient. Trace identifies the dual of $\operatorname{Hom}(S,W/S)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}(W/S,S)$, yielding $M_v=T^*X_v$.

The incidence equations $A(W)\subseteq S$, $A(S)=0$ cut out a closed subscheme of $X_v\times\operatorname{End}(W)$. Projection from this product is projective, hence so is $\mu_v$. Its fiber at $0$ is the zero section scheme, and $A^2=0$ everywhere. This agrees with the zero fiber of the affine invariant quotient of the framed data if that quotient is also used: its invariant functions include all entries of $JI$, so the zero fiber forces $A=0$; conversely at $I=0$ the orbit closure under $g=t^{-1}\operatorname{id}_V$ contains the zero datum as $t\to0$, so every invariant function has its zero-datum value. Thus no assertion identifying the entire affine invariant ring is needed.

A framed inclusion $V\hookrightarrow V^+$ requires $I^+=\xi I$ and $J=J^+\xi$, with the identity on $W$. In the quotient model it is exactly $S\subset T$ and a common $A$ satisfying $A(W)\subset S$, $A(T)=0$; conversely these conditions reconstruct the inclusion and its unframed one-dimensional quotient. They describe the vector bundle $\mathcal K_v$ of rank $k=v(w-v-1)$ on $Y_v$. The map $r$ is the quotient projective bundle of the tautological rank-$(v+1)$ bundle on $X_{v+1}$, with fiber $\mathbb P^v$; $q$ is the bundle of lines in $W/\mathcal S$, with fiber $\mathbb P^{w-v-1}$. Hence $\dim Y_v=a_{v+1}+v=a_v+w-v-1$ and $\dim Z_v=\dim Y_v+k=a_v+a_{v+1}$.

A tangent vector to the flag incidence is induced by some $\xi\in\operatorname{End}(W)$, since adapted bases identify the incidence with a transitive $\operatorname{GL}(W)$ orbit. Cotangent vectors $(A_1,A_2)$ annihilate every such tangent vector exactly when $\operatorname{tr}((A_1+A_2)\xi)=0$ for all $\xi$, that is $A_2=-A_1$. Together with the two cotangent conditions this says $\operatorname{im}A_1\subset S$, $A_1(T)=0$. This identifies the conormal fibers, with the asserted sign in the second factor, and the same linear equations identify vector bundles on every chart. In particular $Z_v$ is smooth and closed in the product. For the first projection, $Z_v$ is a closed subvariety of $M_v\times X_{v+1}$ cut out by $S\subset T\subset\ker A$; for the second it is closed in $X_v\times M_{v+1}$ cut out by $\operatorname{im}A\subset S\subset T$. Both are projective projections. Setting either source or target $A$ to zero cuts all fiber coordinates of $\mathcal K_v$, so both inverse images of zero sections are exactly $Y_v$ with its reduced zero-section scheme structure.

An element $h\in\operatorname{GL}(W)$ acts on data by $(I,J)\mapsto(Ih^{-1},hJ)$ and on the quotient by $(S,A)\mapsto(hS,hAh^{-1})$. It acts on flags and on $\operatorname{Hom}(W/T,S)$ by the same transport. The frame quotient, trace pairing, incidence equations and all projections commute with these actions. This proves the equivariance assertions, including the conormal sign identification. The inherited Axiom of Choice supplies bases; the actual chart computations use only finite-dimensional choices.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $W=\mathbb C^w$, $w\ge0$, and the no-arrow
one-vertex quiver. For $0\le v\le w$, stable data are
$I:W\to V$, $J:V\to W$, $\dim V=v$, with $IJ=0$ and $J$ injective;
$g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$ acts by $(gI,Jg^{-1})$. This extends the
$w=1$ convention in [[def-a1-nakajima-framed-quiver-data]]. The algebraic
orbit space is
$$M_v=T^*X_v=\{(S,A):S\in X_v=\operatorname{Gr}(v,W),\ \operatorname{im}A\subseteq S\subseteq\ker A\},$$
under $S=\operatorname{im}J$, $A=JI$. Put $a_v=v(w-v)$, so
$\dim X_v=a_v$, $\dim M_v=2a_v$. The map
$\mu_v:M_v\to\operatorname{End}(W)$, $(S,A)\mapsto A$, is projective;
its zero fiber $L_v=X_v$ is the zero section.

For $0\le v<w$, put $Y_v=\operatorname{Fl}(v,v+1;W)$ and write
$q:Y_v\to X_v$, $r:Y_v\to X_{v+1}$. The framed subdatum Hecke locus is
$$Z_v=\{(S\subset T,A):\operatorname{im}A\subseteq S,\ T\subseteq\ker A\} =\operatorname{Tot}\mathcal K_v,\qquad \mathcal K_v=\operatorname{Hom}(W/\mathcal T,\mathcal S).$$
Its image in $M_v\times M_{v+1}$ uses the same $A$ in both factors.
It is the conormal bundle to $Y_v\subset X_v\times X_{v+1}$ after applying
fiberwise negation in the second cotangent factor. Both projections are
projective, $\dim Z_v=a_v+a_{v+1}$, and
$Z_v\cap\operatorname{pr}_1^{-1}(L_v)=Y_v
=Z_v\cap\operatorname{pr}_2^{-1}(L_{v+1})$ scheme-theoretically.
All these constructions are $\operatorname{GL}(W)$-equivariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the smooth
normal-sequence suppliers. Fix a field $k$; all schemes and base changes below
are locally of finite type over $k$, and all morphisms are $k$-morphisms. Let $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$ be a regular closed
embedding of codimension $d$ with normal bundle $N$. In particular a closed
embedding of smooth schemes of constant codimension is regular. For any
$f:Y'\to Y$, put $X'=X\times_YY'$ and $N'=N|_{X'}$. The pulled-back ideal gives
a closed immersion $a:C_{X'}Y'\hookrightarrow N'$. Define
$$i^!_{Y'}=(p'^*)^{-1}a_*\sigma_{X'/Y'}:A_m(Y')\longrightarrow A_{m-d}(X'),$$
using [[def-deformation-to-the-normal-cone-and-specialization]] and
[[lem-vector-bundle-chow-homotopy-invariance]]. No fibre product of deformation
spaces over $\mathbb P^1$ with a fictitious map to $Y$ is used. The same
construction for a regular locally closed embedding uses restriction to an open
in which it is closed; the operations agree under further restriction and
extension of cycles, so this is intrinsic.

For $h:Y''\to Y'$ and $h_X:X''=X\times_YY''\to X'$, properness of $h$ gives
$i^!_{Y'}h_*=(h_X)_*i^!_{Y''}$, and flatness of $h$ of fixed pure relative dimension gives
$i^!_{Y''}h^*=h_X^*i^!_{Y'}$. These do not require the base-changed embedding to
be regular. If $X'\hookrightarrow Y'$ is regular with normal bundle
$N_0\subset N'$ and excess bundle $Q=N'/N_0$, then
$i^!_{Y'}=c_{d-\operatorname{rank}N_0}(Q)\cap (i')^!$. In particular
$i^!i_*\alpha=c_d(N)\cap\alpha$. Here $c_j$ means the already defined
operational Chern operator of
[[lem-operational-chern-classes-and-whitney-formula]]; it later becomes the

derivations.claim: The source zero-section embedding has codimension $a_v$ and normal bundle $\operatorname{pr}_1^*T^*X_v$. Its pullback to $Z_v$ is the zero section $Y_v\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Tot}\mathcal K_v$, with normal bundle $\mathcal K_v$ of rank $k=v(w-v-1)$. The normal map is the fiber inclusion of common $A$ into $q^*T^*X_v$. There is a canonical exact sequence $$0\longrightarrow\mathcal K_v\longrightarrow q^*T^*X_v \longrightarrow\Omega_{Y_v/X_{v+1}}\longrightarrow0.$$ Indeed tangent vectors to an $r$-fiber move $S$ inside fixed $T$; restriction of cotangent forms is the surjection dual to $T_{Y_v/X_{v+1}}\hookrightarrow q^*T X_v$. Its kernel consists exactly of $A:W/S\to S$ annihilating $T/S$, namely $\operatorname{Hom}(W/T,S)$. Thus the excess has rank $a_v-k=v$. The excess formula [F2] gives the first intersection class, of dimension $\dim Y_v-v=a_{v+1}$.

For any quotient projective bundle $p:\mathbb P(B)\to T$ of rank $n+1$, put $h=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$. Its relative Euler sequence is $$0\longrightarrow\Omega_p\longrightarrow p^*B\otimes\mathcal O(-1) \longrightarrow\mathcal O\longrightarrow0.$$ The middle map evaluates the tautological quotient after tensoring by its inverse line; its kernel is the relative cotangent bundle, as one checks on a chart where one quotient coordinate is $1$. field $k$, and all morphisms are $k$-morphisms.

normal-sequence suppliers. The operations $c(Z,T,N)$ of
[[lem-gysin-specialization-bivariant-and-base-change]] commute with every
bivariant operation. Given $Z\subset Y\subset T$ and virtual normal bundles
fitting into $0\to N_{Z/Y}\to N_{Z/T}\to N_{Y/T}|_Z\to0$ compatible with the
conormal maps, $c(Z,T,N_{Z/T})=c(Z,Y,N_{Z/Y})c(Y,T,N_{Y/T})$. For regular

the projection pullback; in particular a regular section of a smooth morphism
gives $s^!p^*=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the
proper/quasi-finite and scheme base-change suppliers. Let $k$ be a field and let
$f:X\to Y$ be a proper morphism of schemes locally of finite type over $k$
([[def-proper-morphism]], [[def-locally-finite-type-and-finite-type-morphism]]).
For an integral closed subscheme $V\subseteq X$ with generic point $\eta$, let
$W=\overline{f(V)}\subseteq Y$ with the reduced structure, an integral closed
subscheme ([[def-scheme-theoretic-image]], [[thm-proper-morphism-closed-image]]).
Define
$$f_*[V]:=\begin{cases} [k(V):k(W)]\cdot[W], & \dim W=\dim V,\\ 0, & \dim W<\dim V,\end{cases}$$
where $k(V)$, $k(W)$ are the function fields ([[def-sheaf-total-quotient-rings]])
and $[k(V):k(W)]$ is the extension degree
([[def-extension-degree-and-finite-extension]]), finite because a dominant
morphism $V\to W$ of integral finite-type $k$-schemes with $\dim V=\dim W$ has
algebraic, hence finite, function field extension. Extending $\mathbb Z$-linearly
gives $f_*:Z_d(X)\to Z_d(Y)$ for all $d$. Then:

1. $f_*$ is a homomorphism of graded groups and
   $f_*(\operatorname{Rat}_d(X))\subseteq\operatorname{Rat}_d(Y)$, so it
   descends to $f_*:A_d(X)\to A_d(Y)$
   ([[def-chow-group-of-cycles-mod-rational-equivalence]]).
2. (Functoriality) $\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id}$ and
   $(g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*$ for proper $f,g$; the degree is multiplicative in
   towers of finite function-field extensions.
3. (Base change) For a cartesian square with $g$ flat of pure relative dimension $n$
   and proper $f$, the
   compatibility of lem-pushforward-pullback-compatibility-chow holds.

$d+1$ and $r\in k(W)^*$ one has
$$f_*\bigl(\operatorname{div}_W(r)\bigr)=\operatorname{div}_{f(W)}\bigl(N_{k(W)/k(f(W))}(r)\bigr)$$
when $\dim f(W)=\dim W$, and $f_*(\operatorname{div}_W(r))=0$ when
$\dim f(W)<\dim W$; here $N$ is the field norm.

derivations.claim: The projections of $R_{uv}$ to either factor are projective by base change from $\mu_v$ or $\mu_u$. The intersection support defining $D\star C$ lies in $M_u\times_{\operatorname{End}(W)}M_v \times_{\operatorname{End}(W)}M_t$; forgetting the middle factor is projective by base change from $\mu_v$, so $p_{13}$ is proper there. The support for $C\star\alpha$ lies in $L_u\times L_v$ and projects properly to $L_v$ because $L_u$ is projective. The diagonals of the smooth $M_v$ and $M_u$ are regular of codimensions $2a_v$ and $2a_u$. Refined Gysin and pushforward therefore define the stated homomorphisms with exactly the displayed degree shifts.

For three kernels on consecutive pairs, place their external product on the six-factor product, and impose the two identifications of the repeated middle varieties by refined diagonal Gysins. The two regular embeddings use independent factors; their refined operations commute and their composite is the common double-diagonal operation by [F2]. Either parenthesization of convolution is this operation followed by forgetting the two middle factors. To move each intermediate pushforward past the remaining Gysin, use the proper base-change compatibility in [F2] on the common-endomorphism support; properness was checked in step 1.1. Functoriality [F3] then identifies the two expressions, proving associativity without a transversality assertion for the kernels.

Place $\alpha$, $C$ and $D$ on the corresponding five-factor product. The same argument imposes first the source and then the middle diagonal, or in the opposite order, with the same final projection to $L_t$. This proves the action identity. For a diagonal kernel the imposed middle equality is a regular section of a smooth projection; its refined Gysin cancels that projection's flat pullback by [F2], so the resulting operation is the identity. This proves the unit assertions as well.

Since $L_u$ and $M_u$ are smooth and $L_u\hookrightarrow M_u$ is a zero section, the diagonal intersection with $[L_u]\times C$ equals the base-changed zero-section Gysin on $C$. In local smooth coordinates this is the graph equality followed by the equations for that zero section; Gysin composition [F2] identifies it with the single regular embedding $L_u\times M_v\hookrightarrow M_u\times M_v$. The resulting classes remain supported on $L_v$ by step 1.1. Finally transport by $h\in\operatorname{GL}(W)$ preserves the common-endomorphism supports, all diagonals and all projection maps by [F1]. Proper and Gysin naturality [F2]–[F3] therefore intertwine the induced ordinary Chow actions. This proves the final assertions.

derivations.claim: The top-dimensional Chow group of an irreducible $a_v$-dimensional variety is freely generated by its fundamental class: there is only one integral subvariety of dimension $a_v$, and rational equivalences in this degree would require an $(a_v+1)$-dimensional subvariety, which does not exist. Thus $\mathcal V_w$ has basis $b_0,\ldots,b_w$. By [F1]–[F3] the Hecke operators have exactly the required degree to preserve these top summands, and their actual push-pull actions are the raw coefficients of [F2]. Since $a_v-a_{v+1}=2v+1-w$, the reverse sign has parity $w-1$; multiplying it into the raw reverse coefficient gives $(-1)^{w-1+w-v-1}(w-v)=(-1)^v(w-v)$. This proves all displayed coefficient formulas.

For $0\le v\le w$, the formulas in step 1.1 give $EF b_v=(v+1)(w-v)b_v$ and $FE b_v=v(w-v+1)b_v$, with the same equalities at the endpoints by zero extension. Their difference is $(w-2v)b_v=Hb_v$. Since $E$ raises the $H$-weight by $2$ and $F$ lowers it by $2$, the same formulas give $[H,E]=2E$ and $[H,F]=-2F$ on every basis vector. They are the defining brackets of the trace-zero two-by-two Lie algebra, so these operators extend to its enveloping-algebra representation. This is a correspondence action: [F3] identifies every product of its geometric kernels with the corresponding composite operator, so the computed relations are relations of that action rather than formal dimension matching.

The vector $b_0$ is killed by $E$ and has weight $w$. Successive lowering gives $F^v b_0=(-1)^{v(v-1)/2}v!b_v$, which is nonzero for $0\le v\le w$; thus it generates the whole space. Both $E$ and $F$ are nilpotent since they move among finitely many summands. If a nonzero invariant subspace is given, a polynomial in the diagonal $H$ projects a nonzero vector onto one of its distinct weight components $\mathbb Q b_v$; applying $E^v$ gives a nonzero multiple of $b_0$, and then the powers of $F$ give all basis vectors. This proves irreducibility and integrability, including the trivial one-dimensional module at $w=0$. Replacing $b_v$ by $(-1)^{v(v-1)/2}b_v$ gives the usual divided-power coefficients $F c_v=(v+1)c_{v+1}$ and $E c_v=(w-v+1)c_{v-1}$.

Equivariance follows from [F1]–[F3]; in fact each $h$ sends the entire $L_v$ to itself and hence fixes $b_v$, so it acts trivially on the ordinary top Chow representation. At $w=1$ all spaces and the Hecke correspondence are points and the formulas reduce to the existing fundamental two-dimensional example. This preserves that example as a special case and completes the arbitrary-framing construction.
